{{DISPLAYTITLE:The compiler and runtime}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Programs and proofs in one language}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A Lean definition is used in two ways. The Lean kernel checks it as a term of the type theory,
and the compiler turns it into machine code that runs. The two paths start from the same
definition and, except in the cases described at the end of this page, do not meet again.
This page follows the second path in Lean 4.34.1: from a definition through the compiler's
intermediate representations to C, the run-time system's reference counting and its updates
in place, the attributes that let compiled code differ from the definition the Lean kernel
sees, and what all of this adds to what has to be trusted.

== Two consumers of one definition ==

When a definition is elaborated, the result goes two ways. The compiler receives it with its
recursion intact; the Lean kernel receives a version in which recursion has been expressed
through recursors or well-founded recursion and can be checked.<ref name="rm-ec">"Elaboration and Compilation", a chapter of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0), sections "Elaboration Results" and "Compilation". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/]</ref>
Before generating code, the compiler erases proofs, which have no run-time
content.<ref name="cade">Leonardo de Moura and Sebastian Ullrich, "The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language (System Description)", in ''Automated Deduction: CADE 28'', Lecture Notes in Computer Science 12699, Springer, 2021, pp. 625–635, section 3. doi:[https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37 10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37]; author's copy [https://lean-lang.org/papers/lean4.pdf lean-lang.org/papers/lean4.pdf].</ref>
The compiled code is never shown to the Lean kernel. A theorem about a function is a theorem
about the definition; that the machine code computes the same function is a property of the
compiler, not something the Lean kernel has checked.

== From definitions to C ==

Lean's notes for version 4.22.0, of 14 August 2025, state that "the old compiler has been
replaced by the new compiler".<ref name="rn422">"Lean 4.22.0", in "Release Notes", ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0), Highlights, "New compiler". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/releases/v4.22.0/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/releases/v4.22.0/]</ref>
In 4.34.1 that compiler, written in Lean, is the one in use. It works in stages:

# The elaborated definition is translated into '''LCNF''', the Lean Compiler Normal Form, a representation in A-normal form in which every intermediate result is bound to a name.<ref name="lcnf">Module documentation of <code>Lean.Compiler.LCNF.Basic</code>, "Lean Compiler Normal Form (LCNF)", Lean API documentation. [https://lean-lang.org/doc/api/Lean/Compiler/LCNF/Basic.html lean-lang.org/doc/api/Lean/Compiler/LCNF/Basic.html]</ref>
# Later passes, still over LCNF, make allocation, reference-count updates and memory reuse explicit instructions. The result is also translated into the compiler's '''IR''', the form that Lean prints on request (below).<ref name="src-compiler">Lean 4 source code, version 4.34.1 (2026), directory <code>src/Lean/Compiler/LCNF</code>: in <code>Passes.lean</code> the passes of the impure phase (<code>insertResetReuse</code>, <code>inferBorrow</code>, <code>explicitBoxing</code>, <code>explicitRc</code>, <code>expandResetReuse</code>), in <code>Main.lean</code> the translation of their result to IR (<code>IR.toIR</code>), and <code>EmitC.lean</code>, which emits C. Apache License 2.0. https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/tree/v4.34.1/src/Lean/Compiler/LCNF</ref><ref name="rm-rc">"Reference Counting", section 12.2 of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0), including 12.2.2 "Compiler IR". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Run-Time-Code/Reference-Counting/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Run-Time-Code/Reference-Counting/]</ref>
# The same result is emitted as C. Each Lean module becomes a C file, which a C compiler shipped with Lean compiles to native code.<ref name="src-compiler" /><ref name="rm-ec" />

When Lean evaluates code while processing a file, as <code>#eval</code> does, an
interpreter runs the IR, and switches to native code for any function that has been
compiled ahead of time, which includes the standard library.<ref name="cade" /><ref name="rm-ec" />

The IR of a definition can be printed. This function adds one to every element of a list.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
set_option trace.compiler.ir.result true in
def incAll : List Nat → List Nat
  | [] => []
  | x :: xs => (x + 1) :: incAll xs
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 prints:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">[Compiler.IR] [result]
    def incAll (x_1 : tobj) : tobj :=
      case x_1 : tobj of
      List.nil →
        ret x_1
      List.cons →
        let x_2 : tobj := proj[0] x_1;
        let x_3 : tobj := proj[1] x_1;
        block_4 (x_5 : tobj) (x_6 : u8) :=
          let x_7 : tagged := 1;
          let x_8 : tobj := Nat.add x_2 x_7;
          dec x_2;
          let x_9 : tobj := incAll x_3;
          block_10 (x_11 : obj) :=
            ret x_11;
          case x_6 : u8 of
          Bool.false →
            set x_5[1] := x_9;
            set x_5[0] := x_8;
            jmp block_10 x_5
          Bool.true →
            let x_12 : obj := ctor_1[List.cons] x_8 x_9;
            jmp block_10 x_12;
        let x_13 : u8 := isShared x_1;
        case x_13 : u8 of
        Bool.false →
          jmp block_4 x_1 x_13
        Bool.true →
          inc x_3;
          inc x_2;
          dec x_1;
          jmp block_4 ◾ x_13</pre>

The same definition, given to <code>lean -c</code>, yields a C function. In an excerpt, the
test, the call to the C implementation of addition and the two ways of producing the new
cell read:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">v_isSharedCheck_13_ = !lean_is_exclusive(v_x_1_);
…
v___x_8_ = lean_nat_add(v_head_2_, v___x_7_);
…
if (v_isShared_6_ == 0)
{
lean_ctor_set(v___x_5_, 1, v___x_9_);
lean_ctor_set(v___x_5_, 0, v___x_8_);
…
v_reuseFailAlloc_12_ = lean_alloc_ctor(1, 2, 0);</pre>

== Reference counting and update in place ==

Lean manages memory by '''reference counting'''. Every object on the heap carries a count of
the references to it; the count rises when a reference is copied and falls when one is
dropped, and an object whose count reaches zero is freed at once.<ref name="rm-rc" /> The
traditional objection to reference counting in functional languages is its cost.
Ullrich and de Moura's answer is that an exact count is also information: it says whether a
value is '''shared''', and a value that is not shared may be changed in place without any
observer being able to tell.<ref name="beans">Sebastian Ullrich and Leonardo de Moura, "Counting Immutable Beans: Reference Counting Optimized for Purely Functional Programming", in ''Proceedings of the 31st Symposium on Implementation and Application of Functional Languages (IFL 2019)'', ACM, 2019, article 3, pp. 1–12. doi:[https://doi.org/10.1145/3412932.3412935 10.1145/3412932.3412935]; preprint [https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.05647 arXiv:1908.05647].</ref>

The IR above shows the mechanism. <code>isShared x_1</code> tests the count of the incoming
list cell. If the cell is not shared, the branch <code>Bool.false</code> overwrites its two
fields with <code>set</code> and returns the same cell: the old list is updated in place.
If it is shared, <code>ctor_1[List.cons]</code> allocates a new cell and the old one is left
for its other owners. In the paper this pair of steps is a <code>reset</code> instruction,
which drops an unshared value's references to its fields but keeps its cell, followed by
<code>reuse</code>, which places the new constructor in that cell. The authors observe that
many objects die just before an object of the same kind is created, which they call the
'''resurrection hypothesis''', and that a function such as <code>map</code> applied to an
unshared list therefore allocates no memory at all.<ref name="beans" /> In the Lean 4 system
description this is presented as a programming style, '''functional but in place''': code
is written as pure functions, and runs with destructive updates wherever values are not
shared.<ref name="cade" />

Arrays and strings follow the same rule. Their primitive operations modify the value in place
when they hold the only reference, and copy it otherwise.<ref name="rm-rc" /><ref name="beans" />
Two further techniques keep the cost down. '''Borrowed''' parameters, which a function uses
without consuming, need no count updates, and the compiler infers many of them; and values
reachable from only one thread use cheaper, unsynchronised count updates. Reference counting
cannot reclaim cycles, but the part of Lean that can be reasoned about cannot create
cyclic data, so the runtime has no cycle collector.<ref name="rm-rc" /><ref name="beans" />

== Code that differs from its definition ==

Two attributes let the code that runs differ from the definition that the Lean kernel checks.

'''<code>@[extern "sym"]</code>''' binds a definition to a C symbol: compiled code calls the C
function <code>sym</code> instead of code generated from the definition.<ref name="rm-ffi">"Foreign Function Interface", section 12.4 of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Run-Time-Code/Foreign-Function-Interface/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Run-Time-Code/Foreign-Function-Interface/]</ref>
Addition of natural numbers is an example. The definition of <code>Nat.add</code>, the one
theorems are about, is by recursion on the unary representation (zero and successor);
compiled code calls <code>lean_nat_add</code>, as in the C above. At run time a natural
number is either a small value stored directly in the machine word or a pointer to a
multi-precision number.<ref name="rm-ffi" /> Lean reports the binding:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
import Lean
open Lean

#eval show CoreM (Option String) from do
  return getExternNameFor (← getEnv) `c ``Nat.add
</pre>

This prints <code>some "lean_nat_add"</code>.

'''<code>@[implemented_by f]</code>''' replaces a definition by another Lean function
<code>f</code> in compiled code. Lean's own documentation of the attribute states that "the
provided implementation is not checked to be equivalent to the original
definition".<ref name="impl">Documentation of <code>Lean.Compiler.implementedByAttr</code>, Lean API documentation. [https://lean-lang.org/doc/api/Lean/Compiler/ImplementedByAttr.html lean-lang.org/doc/api/Lean/Compiler/ImplementedByAttr.html]</ref>
Nothing prevents a wrong one.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def alwaysZero (_ : Nat) : Nat := 0

@[implemented_by alwaysZero]
def ident (n : Nat) : Nat := n

#eval ident 5

theorem ident_five : ident 5 = 5 := rfl
</pre>

<code>#eval</code> prints <code>0</code>, and the theorem that <code>ident 5 = 5</code> is
accepted. Both are correct by their own lights: <code>#eval</code> ran the code the compiler
was told to use, and the Lean kernel checked the definition. The most common uses, according to
the same documentation, are to give an efficient unsafe implementation of a function whose
definition is simple to reason about, and to make an unsafe function callable from safe
code.<ref name="impl" /> A safer variant,
<code>@[csimp]</code>, makes the same substitution only on the strength of a proved
equation between the two functions.<ref name="impl" />

== What it adds to what has to be trusted ==

For a proof, ordinarily nothing. Apart from one deprecated primitive,
<code>Lean.reduceBool</code>, whose use <code>#print axioms</code> reports as the axiom
<code>Lean.trustCompiler</code>, the Lean kernel never runs compiled code,<ref name="src-core">Lean 4 source code, version 4.34.1 (2026), file <code>src/Init/Core.lean</code>: the documentation of <code>Lean.reduceBool</code> ("When the kernel tries to reduce a term <code>Lean.reduceBool c</code>, it will invoke the Lean interpreter to evaluate <code>c</code>"), deprecated since 2026-02-01, and of <code>Lean.trustCompiler</code> and <code>Lean.ofReduceBool</code>. Apache License 2.0. https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/v4.34.1/src/Init/Core.lean</ref> so neither the
compiler nor any <code>@[extern]</code> or <code>@[implemented_by]</code> annotation is
consulted when a theorem is checked. The theorem <code>ident_five</code> above holds whatever
the compiled code does.

For a program, everything above is trusted: the compiler, the C compiler, the runtime, and the
claim behind every <code>@[extern]</code> and <code>@[implemented_by]</code> that the code
computes what the definition says. A proof about a function is a proof about the definition.

The two meet in one place. Some tactics, such as <code>decide +native</code> and
<code>bv_decide</code>, prove a statement by running compiled code and admitting its result.
Such a proof depends on the compiler and on every <code>@[extern]</code> and
<code>@[implemented_by]</code> on the path,
and can be wrong when the compiled code disagrees with the definition. Since Lean 4.29.0 each
such computation introduces its own axiom, which <code>#print axioms</code> lists, so the
dependence is visible.<ref name="rm-validating">"Validating a Lean Proof", a chapter of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0), section "On Lean.trustCompiler (up to Lean 4.28.0)". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/]</ref>
[[Lean theorem prover/System/Proof export and independent checkers|Proof export and independent checkers]]
shows the function <code>ident</code> above used to prove a falsehood in exactly this way, and
how the axiom gives it away.
